intro: This guide takes your group through “Talks to the Farmer (For Teens)” in seventeen weeks, one chapter a week. It retells C. H. Spurgeon’s talks on farm life — weeds and walls, ploughing and sowing, frost and harvest — for teens aged about 13 to 18, and every chapter turns an ordinary field into a mirror for the reader’s own life with God. It suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group, and you don’t need to know anything about farming to lead it.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or beforehand at home if your group prefers (8–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own (2–3 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself during the week and decide which question you most want the group to wrestle with. Spurgeon is direct, and several chapters press hard on conscience: hardening your heart, being “almost” a Christian, the weight of sin and the final harvest. Keep pointing to the hope each chapter ends on, and don’t let anyone leave thinking they are beyond God’s reach. The chapters on shearing and threshing speak about loss and hard seasons, so be gentle with anyone who is grieving or going through a difficult time at home, and be ready to talk privately afterwards. Personal reflection in the activities always stays private.

weeks.summary: Solomon walks past a farm overgrown with thorns and nettles, its wall broken down, and stops to learn from it. The owner did nothing wrong to the field; he simply did nothing, and ground left alone always fills with weeds. Spurgeon pictures the sluggard as someone who sincerely means to pray and change and get serious about God “later,” and never starts. The big idea: good intentions grow nothing, so the cure for “later” is to take one real step now.

memory_verse.text: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.

activity.title: The “Later” List
steps: Ask everyone to write down, privately, three things they keep meaning to do with God “one day.”
Have each person circle the one that would make the biggest difference if they actually started it.
Ask them to write the smallest real action they could take on it within the next hour, not a plan but an action.
Invite anyone who wants to say their action aloud, without saying what the bigger thing is.
Agree to ask one another next week, “Did you do it?”

weeks.summary: The sluggard’s stone wall fell down not because anyone attacked it but because he ignored it. Spurgeon names the stones of a Christian’s wall: what you were taught, knowing what you believe, set habits of prayer and Bible reading, being openly a Christian, and the ability to say no. A broken wall costs you the line between yourself and the world, your protection, and in the end the field itself. The big idea: you don’t have to wreck your life to lose it, so put back the one stone that has fallen out, today.

memory_verse.text: A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls.

activity.title: Name the Stones
activity.materials: A whiteboard or large sheet of paper
steps: Draw a long wall made of blank stones on the board.
Ask the group to call out the “stones” Spurgeon lists, and any others they think guard a Christian’s life, and write one in each stone.
Talk about which stones teens most often pull out first, and why.
Ask everyone to decide privately which one stone is missing from their own wall.
Close by asking them to write down for themselves one way to put that stone back this week.

weeks.summary: Spurgeon points out that the Bible says God himself sends the frost and the thaw with a word. He uses the two seasons as a picture of how God works on a heart: first the cold truth about ourselves that freezes our excuses, then the warm wind of forgiveness that melts us. Frost on its own only hardens a person into despair, but the God who sends the cold fully intends to send the thaw, as he did for the thief on the cross. The big idea: feeling caught out and guilty is meant to be the first half of the story, not the end of it.

memory_verse.text: He sends out his word, and melts them; he makes his wind blow and the waters flow.

activity.title: Two-Part Weather
steps: Draw two columns on a sheet and head them “Frost” and “Thaw.”
As a group, list what the chapter says belongs to each: what the frost does, and what the thaw brings.
Ask: what happens to a person who gets the frost but never the thaw? Talk about it together.
Read Isaiah 44:22 aloud and ask which column it belongs in.
Give everyone a moment to write privately the prayer from the chapter in their own words: “God, I can’t melt my own heart.”

weeks.summary: When outsiders ask to see Jesus, he says a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die, or it remains alone. Spurgeon says Jesus is speaking first about himself: the heart of Christianity is not his teaching or example but his death, which brings a harvest of people to life. Then the law turns to us: grip your life and you lose it; let it go and you keep it. The big idea: what we bury for God, especially our need to come first, is what bears much fruit.

memory_verse.text: Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

activity.title: The Upside-Down Ranking
steps: Write these on slips: “getting the credit,” “having the last word,” “being first,” “being noticed,” “keeping my options open,” “looking good online.”
In small groups, rank them from easiest to hardest to let go of.
Compare rankings and talk about why some are harder than others.
Ask each person to choose privately one they will deliberately let go of this week, and to watch what grows there.

weeks.summary: The ploughman really does plough all day, and Spurgeon sees in that God’s patience, working on a heart for years, and the patience we need when we try to reach others. But the ploughman doesn’t only plough: the point of breaking the ground is to sow it. Many people stay stirred and convicted for years without ever trusting Jesus, like someone who reaches the platform just as the train pulls out. The big idea: don’t stay “almost” a Christian; tumble into Christ’s arms, however clumsily.

memory_verse.text: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

activity.title: Ploughing or Planting?
steps: Read out these statements one at a time: “I felt moved at camp,” “I know I should pray more,” “I asked Jesus to forgive me,” “I cried in a service,” “I told God I trust him,” “I meant to sort things out with God.”
For each one, the group decides whether it is ploughing (being stirred) or planting (actually trusting) and says why.
Talk about why it is easy to mistake ploughing for planting.
Read the young man’s words and Spurgeon’s answer from the chapter, and ask what “tumble into them” means.
Give a quiet minute for anyone who wants to tell God privately that they are moving from “almost” to “yes.”

weeks.summary: Nobody ploughs solid rock, and Spurgeon warns that a heart can go like that. It usually hardens not through rebellion but by hearing the truth so often that it stops landing: “the sun that softens wax hardens clay.” God’s patient work has a limit, and the chances to respond can quietly end. Yet the chapter ends in hope: if it bothers you that your heart feels hard, you are not stone yet. The big idea: act on whatever soft spot God has given you, today, rather than giving your heart one more reason to shrug.

memory_verse.text: And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.

activity.title: Wax or Clay?
steps: Read Spurgeon’s line “The sun that softens wax hardens clay” and ask the group what it means in their own words.
Brainstorm together the ways a teen who grew up around church can become “expert at feeling nothing.”
Talk about Spurgeon’s fisherman with no hooks: why truth that never stings cannot rescue anyone.
Ask each person to write privately one small way they will act this week on something God has stirred in them.

weeks.summary: In Jesus’ parable the same sower throws the same good seed onto four kinds of ground: the hard path, thin soil over rock, ground full of thorns, and good soil. Spurgeon shows each as a kind of hearer: the distracted mind where nothing sinks in, the quick enthusiast with no roots, the believer whose faith is choked by worry, money and pleasure, and the person who bears fruit, whether a lot or a little. The parable is a mirror, not a lecture, and ground can be broken up. The big idea: the question is not whether the message is true but what kind of ground we are, and God can turn a path into a field.

memory_verse.text: As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.

activity.title: Four Fields Today
activity.materials: Four sheets of paper labelled Path, Rock, Thorns and Good Soil
steps: Put the four sheets in four corners of the room.
Read out modern situations, such as “scrolling through a sermon video,” “dropping out after friends laughed,” “too busy with exams and work to pray,” and “quietly helping at home because of Jesus.”
Have the group walk to the corner they think fits each one, and talk about any disagreements.
Ask everyone to think privately about which field they have mostly been standing in lately, without saying it aloud.
Close by reading the hopeful line: “He’s in the business of turning paths into fields.”

weeks.summary: A wise farmer decides what his main crop is and gives it the best field. Spurgeon says everyone has a main crop, chosen or not, and argues that knowing God belongs in the best field because it is the most necessary thing and the only crop that pays in this life and the next. He warns against keeping faith but starving it, like the father who “hasn’t worked much at it lately,” and calls worldly success “only smoke.” The big idea: give God your best soil, not your leftovers, because you were made to know him.

memory_verse.text: But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

activity.title: What Gets the Best Field?
steps: Ask each person to draw a simple farm map with one large “best field” and several small plots.
Have them write privately what actually fills each field in their week, judging by where their time and attention go.
Discuss as a group: why do the things in our best field often end up there by default?
Ask everyone to decide privately one change that would move knowing God toward the best field this week.

weeks.summary: In early spring the first green blade of wheat is tiny and easy to miss, but it is the start of the harvest. Spurgeon says the first stirrings of God in a person look like that: a faint desire for God, a prayer that is only a sigh, wanting to be where God is talked about. God sees and waters these small beginnings, as shepherds watch over newborn lambs, and older Christians should treat younger ones gently. The big idea: small faith is not fake faith; God delights in the blossom and finishes what he starts.

memory_verse.text: And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.

activity.title: Spot the Green Blades
steps: As a group, list every sign of “green blade” faith the chapter mentions.
Add any other small, real signs of faith the group can think of.
Talk about how older Christians can stamp on green blades without meaning to, and how teens can protect them in each other.
Ask everyone to write privately one green blade they can see in their own life, and to thank God for it.

weeks.summary: Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Spurgeon draws two truths: we are workers on God’s farm, each with our own job, so no one can boast of a convert; and we cannot do the main part at all, because only God gives new life. Like the child who digs up seeds to check them, we often give up on people too soon, but some of the best things grow slowest. The big idea: do your faithful part, then rest and leave the growing to God.

memory_verse.text: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.

activity.title: Planters and Waterers
steps: Ask the group to list the planting jobs (starting a conversation, an invitation) and watering jobs (follow-up, kindness, example) mentioned or implied in the chapter.
Have each person decide whether they are more naturally a planter or a waterer, and share if they wish.
Ask each person to write privately the name of one person they have been anxious about.
Have them write one faithful thing they will do for that person this week, and then a short prayer handing the result to God.

weeks.summary: Isaiah foresaw Jesus standing silent before his accusers like a sheep before its shearers, holding back his power on purpose. Spurgeon then applies the picture to us: God sometimes shears his people, cutting away things they love. A sheep is hurt more by struggling than by the shears, the shearer picks the right season, what is cut away was only on loan, and new wool grows. The big idea: in a hard season we can lie still in the hands of the Shepherd who only cuts what it is time to let go.

memory_verse.text: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.

activity.title: On Loan
steps: Read the four lessons of the shearing aloud and list them on paper: struggling hurts more, the season is chosen, it was on loan, new wool grows.
Ask the group which of the four they find most comforting and which most difficult, and why.
Ask each person to write privately a list of five good things in their life, and to write “on loan” beside each one.
Close by reading the prayer “Lord, if this has to come, sanctify it” and inviting everyone to pray it silently about anything hard they can see coming.

weeks.summary: Spurgeon builds a chapter on grass. “Nature” is just a word we use to avoid saying God, who personally causes the grass to grow, even for cattle that can never thank him. He grows grass on lonely mountainsides seen only by a bird, and gives every blade its own drop of dew, as Mungo Park was comforted by a tiny patch of moss in the desert. The big idea: God’s care is personal and particular, so the hidden, unnoticed person is not forgotten.

memory_verse.text: But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?

activity.title: A Drop of Dew
activity.materials: Nothing (or a short walk outside if the weather allows)
steps: If you can, step outside for five minutes and have each person find one small living thing nobody else would notice.
Come back together and let each person say what they found.
Ask: what does God’s care for that small thing say about his care for people who feel invisible?
Ask everyone to think privately of a time they have felt unseen, and to tell God about it in a silent prayer.

weeks.summary: Harvest meant a feast and real joy, and the Bible uses it as a picture of deep gladness. But the harvest also means you reap what you sow. Spurgeon tells of his own conversion as a hard ploughing by the Ten Commandments followed by hope and assurance, and lists the harvest joys of telling others, answered prayer, beating temptation and, greatest of all, helping someone find God. The big idea: the joys of God outshine everything the world sells, so plant now for the harvest you want to reap.

memory_verse.text: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.

activity.title: Rank the Harvest Joys
steps: Write Spurgeon’s harvest joys on slips: forgiveness, telling someone else, answered prayer, beating a temptation, helping someone find God.
In small groups, rank them from the joy you have tasted most to the one you have tasted least.
Read Spurgeon’s line about Gabriel’s throne and ask why he valued that last joy so highly.
Talk about the ripe stalk that bows its head: what does humble, mature faith look like in a teenager?
Ask each person to choose privately one harvest joy to aim for this month.

weeks.summary: Ruth was poor, widowed and foreign, gleaning leftover grain, but Boaz let her gather among the sheaves and quietly had extra dropped for her. Spurgeon says that is how God treats the unsure believer: welcome in the middle of the field of his promises. The one condition is to stoop, because proud people go home empty, and what we gather must then be “chewed” over slowly to feed us, and shared with others. The big idea: God’s riches are within reach of anyone humble enough to bend, and they feed us when we take time to digest them.

memory_verse.text: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

activity.title: Crop or Chew?
activity.materials: A Bible and paper and pens
steps: Ask the group how many Bible verses or Christian posts they think they see in a typical week, and how many they remember.
Read one short verse together, then ask everyone to write it down from memory.
Spend three minutes in silence turning it over: what does each phrase mean, and why does it matter?
Ask a few people to share one thing they noticed the second time that they missed the first.
Challenge everyone to come back to that verse three separate times this week, and to pass it on to one person.

weeks.summary: In Amos God says he is pressed down like a cart overloaded with sheaves, and the weight is our sin. Spurgeon notes that the whole universe is no strain for God, yet sin is the one thing described as almost too heavy to bear, especially pointless sin. Then the chapter turns: in Jesus, from Gethsemane to the cross, God climbed under the wagon and carried the load himself. The big idea: sin is far heavier than we think, and Jesus has already carried it for anyone who will hand it to him.

memory_verse.text: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.

activity.title: Weights and Measures
steps: Ask the group to list things people their age treat as “no big deal” that God takes seriously.
Discuss why we get the weights backwards, as Spurgeon says.
Read 1 Peter 2:24 together slowly.
Ask each person to write privately the weight they have been calling light, then to tear the paper up or fold it away as a sign of handing it to Jesus.

weeks.summary: Threshing beat the grain to free it from its husk, and Spurgeon says hard times can be God loosening the husk of sin and selfishness. The farmer only threshes the wheat, not the weeds, he matches the tool to the seed, and he does not thresh forever: if God appoints ten troubles, there will not be eleven. None of it is meant to feel pleasant, and we are allowed to hate it. The big idea: a hard season is not proof that God is against us; it is measured, limited and headed somewhere good.

memory_verse.text: For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

activity.title: Two Promises
steps: Ask the group to find the promises in the chapter for someone in a hard season, and list them together.
Talk about the difference between asking “Why me?” and asking “What husk is this loosening?”
Be clear that it is fine to hate suffering, and that hard times are not always a punishment.
Give each person a card to write the two promises on: “He only threshes the wheat” and “He does not thresh forever,” to keep for themselves or give to someone who is struggling.

weeks.summary: In Jesus’ parable of the wheat and the weeds, both grow together until the harvest, when the wheat is gathered into the barn. Spurgeon reads the line word by word: “but” marks the final sorting; “gather” means rescue, with no true grain lost; “wheat” asks whether our faith was sown by God and depends on Christ; and “into my barn” promises safety forever, so a Christian’s death is a gathering-in. The big idea: make sure you are real wheat, rooted in Christ, and the final harvest is nothing to fear.

memory_verse.text: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

activity.title: Looking Back Over the Field
steps: Ask the group to list as many of the book’s farm pictures as they can remember, from the sluggard’s field to the barn.
Have each person choose the one picture that has stayed with them most and say why, if they are comfortable.
Read Spurgeon’s question about being sown by the Lord or “self-sown,” and give a quiet minute for private reflection.
Ask everyone to write themselves a short note on what they want to keep from this book, and to pray for one another to be gathered in.
